messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir remembered the hotel ballroom as a blur of polished marble and low jazz, the night of the regional therapy conference bleeding into an unmarked elevator ride. The man who cornered him against the service corridor did not speak much; he just pressed a heavy, familiar blend of sandalwood and amber cologne into Amir’s face, the scent so thick it felt like wool stuffed in his nose. When Amir tried to push him away, a sharp, twisting pain bloomed across his right ribs, a somatic anchor that would never truly fade. The forced sexual contact lasted only minutes, but it left a hollow, burning awareness in his pelvis that turned every subsequent moment of physical closeness into a trap, making the olfactory, somatic, and intimate cues he later encountered feel inescapably tied to that original violation. In the weeks that followed, the rehabilitation clinic where Amir worked as a physical therapist became a minefield. When a senior colleague leaned over his desk to discuss a treatment plan, wearing a similar citrus-and-woods fragrance, Amir’s chest tightened until he had to excuse himself to the restroom. The heavy cologne and the familiar ache in his ribs did not just remind him of the night he was violated; they confirmed his worsening belief that he could never rely on himself to stay safe, that his body was permanently marked with shame, and that he would never feel normal emotions again. That conviction did not remain passive. It fed directly into a state of perpetual alarm, his shoulders hiking to his ears the moment a patient’s gurney rolled too quickly down the hall or a colleague reached to pat his shoulder without warning. Because his nervous system constantly braced for sudden impacts, Amir found himself retreating into his own skull. He began pretending these violent encounters were happening to other therapists at conventions, carefully steering his thoughts away from the event while constantly scanning his own frame for new twinges of injury. Every unexpected jolt—the drop of a chart, the sudden turn of a partner in bed—ripped through him as if he were still backing into a wall, and because he could not trust his own reactions to make sense, he began to treat every familiar scent and every shift in physical proximity as an immediate threat, a feedback loop that tightened with every missed shift and every evening spent lying rigid beside his wife, his hand hovering over her arm but never landing. His belief that he was fundamentally damaged did not just spark alarm; it recalibrated his perception, ensuring that ordinary clinic interactions continued to detonate his startle response. The sheer frequency of these false alarms kept his nervous system in overdrive, ensuring that every familiar scent and every shift in physical proximity continued to register as an immediate threat. Avoiding the memory and dissociating from daily sensations meant that no safe experiences could overwrite the trauma, so ordinary cues continued to detonate his startle response, a minor but persistent static that barely registered beneath the louder machinery of his fear. Six months into his marriage, the silence in their bedroom had grown louder than the trauma itself. He had come to believe he would never feel normal emotions again, that any attempt at intimacy would only confirm his damage. The final push to seek treatment came when he dropped a sterile tray during a routine assessment, watching it scatter across the tile while his own heart hammered against his bruised ribs, realizing he was no longer capable of holding his patients or his own life together. He had come to the clinic not to dissect the past, but to find a way to stop flinching from a touch that meant care, hoping, against all his current evidence, to finally trust his own body again.
